from confluent_kafka import Consumer, TopicPartition

# Log-based consumer: controls its own offset (replay from beginning)
conf = {
    'bootstrap.servers': 'kafka:9092',
    'group.id': 'audit-replay-consumer',
    'enable.auto.commit': False,  # manual offset control
    'auto.offset.reset': 'earliest',
}

consumer = Consumer(conf)
topic = 'orders'

# Replay from the very beginning of the log (offset 0)
topic_partitions = consumer.partitions_for_topic(topic)
assignment = [
    TopicPartition(topic, p, 0)  # offset=0: start from beginning
    for p in topic_partitions
]
consumer.assign(assignment)
consumer.seek_to_beginning(assignment)

while True:
    msg = consumer.poll(timeout=1.0)
    if msg is None:
        break
    process(msg.value())
    consumer.commit()  # commit offset only after processing

words.shortDefinition: A CRDT optimisation that propagates only the recent change delta rather than full state, reducing network overhead.
words.simpleDefinition: A delta-state CRDT (δ-CRDT) extends state-based CRDTs by shipping only the small delta — what changed since the last sync — instead of the full state on every gossip round. It preserves the simple network model of state-based CRDTs (at-least-once delivery, no causal ordering required) while dramatically reducing message size for large data structures.
words.longDefinition: Delta-state CRDTs were introduced in a 2016 paper by Paulo Sérgio Almeida, Ali Shoker, and Carlos Baquero as an optimisation to pure state-based (CvRDT) propagation. The core problem with state-based CRDTs is bandwidth: a G-Counter in a 100-node cluster must ship the entire 100-element vector on every gossip round even if only one slot changed. In a δ-CRDT, each mutating operation produces both the updated state and a delta — the minimal state that, when joined with any other replica's state, propagates the change correctly. Replicas exchange deltas (tiny, usually constant-size) rather than full states, and can buffer and batch multiple deltas before shipping. The join operation on deltas is the same semilattice join as for full states — idempotency and commutativity are preserved. This gives δ-CRDTs the best of both worlds: the relaxed network model of CvRDTs (at-least-once delivery) and the small message size of CmRDTs (operation messages). Automerge 2.0 (2023, rewritten in Rust with WASM targets) and Yjs both use delta-based propagation internally. As of 2024–2026, delta-state CRDTs are the dominant implementation approach for production CRDT systems, especially in mobile and peer-to-peer contexts where bandwidth is constrained.
words.connector: Think of a delta-state CRDT like a shared spreadsheet that sends only the changed cells rather than the entire sheet on every keystroke — you get the same eventual result with a fraction of the bandwidth.
words.techContext: Our mobile offline-sync library uses δ-CRDTs so that a user editing a shared document on a low-bandwidth mobile connection sends deltas of under 100 bytes per keystroke rather than the full document state.
words.exampleSentence: Switching from full-state to delta-state CRDT propagation reduced sync bandwidth by 97% for large shared workspaces, making the real-time collaboration feature viable for users on mobile data plans.
words.etymology: Delta (Greek Δ) meaning a small incremental change; state indicating the replication unit is state (not operations); CRDT as before; introduced as δ-CRDT by Almeida, Shoker, and Baquero (2016).

words.shortDefinition: Facebook's XOR-based float compression technique for time-series data that exploits sequential timestamp and value similarity.
words.simpleDefinition: Gorilla compression encodes time-series floating-point values using XOR of consecutive values and variable-length bit packing. Adjacent metric values are typically close together — CPU utilisation at t and t+15s differ by a small delta — so their XOR has many leading zeros, compressing to a handful of bits. Facebook's 2015 VLDB paper reported 12:1 compression ratios, enabling an in-memory time-series store for 2 billion data points.
words.longDefinition: Gorilla was Facebook's in-memory TSDB, described in the 2015 VLDB paper 'Gorilla: A Fast, Scalable, In-Memory Time Series Database'. The key compression insight applies to both timestamps and values. Timestamp compression: rather than storing raw Unix timestamps (8 bytes each), store the delta between consecutive timestamps (usually a constant like 15 seconds in Prometheus scraping), then the delta-of-deltas. If the scrape interval is perfectly regular, the delta-of-delta is 0 and encodes in a single bit. Value compression: store the first value as a raw 64-bit float, then XOR each subsequent value with its predecessor. Because adjacent metric values change slowly (CPU rarely jumps from 40% to 95% in one scrape), the XOR has many leading and trailing zero bits. The non-zero portion (the 'meaningful bits') is variable-length encoded using 5 bits to specify the leading zeros, 6 bits for the length, and then only the meaningful bits. Typical metric values compress from 64 bits to 1.37 bits on average. This technique is now used across the time-series ecosystem: InfluxDB, Prometheus's TSDB (chunks use Gorilla-style encoding), TimescaleDB's columnar compression, QuestDB, and VictoriaMetrics all implement variants of Gorilla-style XOR compression for float columns.
words.connector: Think of Gorilla compression like describing a movie scene by scene — instead of describing each frame in full detail, you say 'same as before except the actor moved 3 pixels left', since adjacent frames are almost identical.
words.techContext: TimescaleDB's Gorilla compression on our metrics table reduced float storage from 8 bytes per value to an average of 1.2 bytes, enabling a 6x increase in in-memory metrics retention within the same RAM budget.
words.exampleSentence: After enabling Gorilla compression on the Prometheus TSDB, the 30-day metrics retention that previously required 2 TB of disk fit in 180 GB — a 11x reduction that allowed us to extend retention to 6 months at the same cost.
words.etymology: Named after the Gorilla TSDB project at Facebook (a playful name for the in-memory beast handling large scale); the compression algorithm described in 'Gorilla: A Fast, Scalable, In-Memory Time Series Database' (Pelkonen et al., VLDB 2015).

words.shortDefinition: A database feature that exposes an ordered stream of all document or row changes for downstream consumers to subscribe to.
words.simpleDefinition: A change feed is a database-native mechanism that continuously emits an ordered log of every insert, update, and delete as it happens. Consumers subscribe to this feed to build derived views, trigger side effects, replicate data to other systems, or implement event-driven architectures — without polling the source database.
words.longDefinition: A change feed is the database-native expression of CDC (Change Data Capture). Rather than an external tool tailing a binary log (Debezium reading MySQL's binlog), a change feed is a first-class database API. DynamoDB Streams is one of the earliest and most widely deployed change feeds: every item-level change in a DynamoDB table is captured in an ordered stream accessible for 24 hours, consumed by Lambda functions or Kinesis. Cosmos DB Change Feed exposes an ordered, persistent log of all document changes per logical partition, used for event sourcing, cache invalidation, and search index synchronisation. CockroachDB's Change Data Capture (CDC, GA 2020) streams row-level changes to Kafka, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, or a webhook in Avro or JSON format with guaranteed ordering per key. MongoDB Change Streams (introduced in 3.6) use the oplog to emit real-time change events; Atlas Stream Processing (2024) connects change streams directly to serverless compute. PostgreSQL 10+ logical replication slots underpin change feeds in Supabase Realtime, Neon branching, and PgBouncer-based CDC solutions. The architectural value of a change feed over polling: it is push-based (no polling interval lag), it captures deletes (polling misses hard deletes), and it is ordered (consumers know the exact sequence of changes).
words.connector: Think of a change feed like subscribing to a database's event log the way you subscribe to a newspaper — instead of checking whether anything changed, you receive each change the moment it is committed.
words.techContext: We subscribe to Cosmos DB's change feed to keep our Elasticsearch search index in sync — every product document update streams to a Function App that re-indexes the document within 2 seconds of the write.
words.exampleSentence: The change feed let the team implement a real-time notification service without polling — users receive push notifications within 500 milliseconds of a relevant document changing in Cosmos DB.

# Azure Cosmos DB: process a change feed in Python
from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
import time

client = CosmosClient(url='https://account.documents.azure.com',
                      credential='<key>')
container = client.get_database_client('mydb') \
                   .get_container_client('orders')

# Read change feed from the beginning
continuation = None
while True:
    response = container.query_items_change_feed(
        is_start_from_beginning=(continuation is None),
        continuation=continuation,
    )
    changes = list(response)
    for change in changes:
        print(f"Changed: {change['id']} status={change.get('status')}")
        # process: update search index, send notification, etc.

    continuation = response.continuation_token
    if not changes:
        time.sleep(1)  # poll when caught up; feed is otherwise push

words.shortDefinition: Running analytical queries in-process alongside application code — e.g. DuckDB — rather than in a separate data warehouse cluster.
words.simpleDefinition: Embedded analytics means running analytical SQL inside the same process as your application code, using a library like DuckDB, rather than sending queries to a separate warehouse cluster over the network. This eliminates the server-provisioning overhead, network round-trips, and billing model of cloud warehouses for workloads that fit on a single machine.
words.longDefinition: Traditional analytics requires a separate server process — a Redshift cluster, a BigQuery project, a Spark cluster — with a network hop from the application to the analytics engine. For a wide class of workloads this is unnecessary overhead: a data engineer transforming 100 GB of Parquet files locally, a backend service computing per-tenant aggregates over its own data, an edge compute node summarising IoT sensor data, or a notebook exploring a dataset client-side. Embedded analytics libraries provide full OLAP capability as a linked library with no server, no port, and no network. DuckDB (CWI Amsterdam, v1.0 2024) is the paradigm-defining tool: import duckdb in Python, Go, R, or Rust and execute vectorised columnar SQL against local Parquet, CSV, S3 objects, PostgreSQL, Arrow in-memory tables, or lakehouse tables (Iceberg, Delta). DuckDB-WASM (2021) takes this further, running full analytical SQL in the browser via WebAssembly. MotherDuck extends the embedded model with optional cloud spill for larger-than-RAM datasets. The distinction from HTAP: embedded analytics runs in the application process (no separate database process); HTAP is a database architecture that handles both workloads in one server. Embedded analytics represents the same architectural shift SQLite made for OLTP in 2000 — eliminating the server as a required deployment unit — but for analytical workloads.
words.connector: Think of embedded analytics like a scientific calculator built into your phone — you get full computational capability wherever you are without connecting to a separate computation server.
words.techContext: Our backend service uses embedded DuckDB to run per-customer analytics queries over pre-staged Parquet files in S3, returning results in 200ms without routing through Redshift and paying per-query costs.
words.exampleSentence: Embedded analytics with DuckDB eliminated the separate BI cluster for internal reporting — the application server queries its own data files in-process and renders dashboards with no additional infrastructure.
